moat_against: Commodity product — no switching costs, no network effects, no lock-in; buyers choose on price, location, rate buydown
No visible pricing power: incentives ~10% of revenue, home-sales gross margin fell 21.8% -> 20.7%
Land/lots bought in a competitive open market (lot costs +5% YoY in Q3 FY2026)
Capable, well-capitalized rivals (Lennar, PulteGroup, NVR — NVR's asset-light model earns structurally higher ROE)
moat_for: #1 U.S. builder by volume since 2002, ~15% national share — procurement and subcontractor scale
Lot discipline: 570,000 lots, only 22% owned / 78% controlled via purchase contracts, plus captive Forestar supply
Balance sheet strength lets it keep building and buying back stock through troughs while small builders starve
Affordability positioning ($362k average closing price) targets the deepest, most undersupplied buyer pool
moat_justification: Largest U.S. builder since 2002 (~15% share, doubled in 10 yrs) with procurement scale, a 570k-lot position only 22% owned / 78% optioned plus captive Forestar supply, and a balance sheet that gains share through downturns — against a commodity product with zero switching costs or network effects, no pricing power (incentives ~10% of revenue, gross margin 21.8% -> 20.7%), open-market land competition, and capable rivals (Lennar, PulteGroup, NVR).
name: D.R. Horton, Inc.
one_liner: America's largest builder with a narrow scale moat (5/10) and a real buyback, but at $135.45 (12.7x TTM OE of $10.63) it returns only 10.1% weighted — it clears the 15% hurdle only at ~$83 (~$62 with a 25% margin of safety); even the bull case is worth less than today's price.
